promptText: Why can't a model reason well about similarity using raw token IDs alone?
options: Token IDs are arbitrary integers assigned by the vocabulary, with no numeric relationship reflecting meaning between related tokens
Token IDs are too large to fit into a neural network's input layer
Token IDs change randomly every time the same word is tokenized
Token IDs can only represent numbers, not words
explanation: Token IDs are arbitrary labels from tokenization; embeddings map them into a learned geometric space specifically designed so that distance and direction correspond to semantic similarity, which raw integer IDs cannot provide on their own.

promptText: What is the key limitation of bag-of-words / one-hot representations that embeddings were designed to fix?
options: They require too much disk space to store word counts
They are synonym-blind: a query for 'physician' cannot match a document that only says 'doctor' because the two words share zero vocabulary positions
They cannot represent punctuation or numbers
They can only be computed offline, never in real time
explanation: Bag-of-words vectors treat every distinct word as an independent, equidistant dimension, so no amount of reweighting (like TF-IDF) can capture synonymy -- the representation itself has no concept of semantic relatedness.

promptText: What is the main difference between a static embedding (like word2vec) and a contextual embedding (like one produced by a Transformer)?
options: Static embeddings are always higher-dimensional than contextual embeddings
A static embedding assigns exactly one fixed vector to a word regardless of context; a contextual embedding computes a different vector depending on the surrounding sentence
Contextual embeddings can only be used for images, not text
Static embeddings require a GPU to compute, while contextual embeddings do not
explanation: word2vec-style models give 'bank' one vector forever regardless of meaning; contextual embeddings compute the vector on the fly via attention, so the same word gets different vectors in 'river bank' versus 'bank account'.

promptText: What does it concretely mean for an embedding model to produce '768-dimensional' vectors?
options: Each embedding is an ordered list of exactly 768 floating-point numbers, regardless of whether the input was one word or several paragraphs
The model can only process inputs up to 768 characters long
The model was trained on exactly 768 example sentences
Each embedding contains 768 separate vectors, one per possible meaning
explanation: Dimensionality is a fixed architectural property tied to the model's hidden-layer size; every output vector has the same fixed length no matter the input length, which is what allows uniform storage and comparison in a vector index.

promptText: What is contrastive learning, in the context of training embedding models?
options: Training the model to predict the next token in a sequence, exactly like a chat model
Showing the model pairs of similar and dissimilar examples and nudging it, via gradient descent, to pull similar pairs' embeddings closer together and push dissimilar pairs' embeddings farther apart
Training two entirely separate models and averaging their outputs
Manually assigning coordinates to each word based on a hand-built thesaurus
explanation: Contrastive learning uses similarity as the training signal itself -- related pairs (a query and its answer, two paraphrases) are pulled together and unrelated pairs are pushed apart, requiring no explicit topic labels.

promptText: Why should the original source text always be stored alongside its embedding vector in a vector database?
options: Storing the text is required by law in most jurisdictions
An embedding is not meaningfully reversible back into readable text, so without the original text you cannot display results or feed retrieved content to an LLM
Vector databases automatically delete vectors that lack accompanying text
The embedding vector alone takes up more storage than the raw text
explanation: Embeddings are a lossy compression of meaning into geometry, not a reversible encoding, so the raw text must be retrievable by ID for anything downstream (showing results, RAG prompting) to work.

promptText: Why is mixing vectors from two different embedding models in the same vector index considered one of the most dangerous production bugs, rather than a minor inconsistency?
options: It causes the vector database to crash immediately, making it easy to catch

Different models produce geometrically unrelated vector spaces, so mixed vectors return similarity scores that look valid (no exception thrown) but are semantically meaningless, silently degrading search quality
It doubles the storage cost of the index with no other effect
Most vector databases automatically detect and reject mismatched models
explanation: Even if dimensionality happens to match, distance and direction in one model's space carry no meaning relative to another model's space, so mixing them produces no error -- only quietly degraded, hard-to-diagnose retrieval quality.

promptText: Why do embeddings often fail to distinguish 'the flight was delayed' from 'the flight was not delayed'?
options: Embedding models cannot process the word 'not' at all
The two sentences share nearly identical surrounding vocabulary and topic, and embeddings are trained primarily to capture topical/semantic similarity rather than precise logical polarity
Negation words are always removed during tokenization
This never actually happens with modern contextual embedding models
explanation: Because contrastive training signals mostly reward topical closeness, a sentence and its negation -- which share almost all the same words -- can end up close together in embedding space despite having opposite truth values, so systems needing precise polarity should not rely on embedding similarity alone.

promptText: Why did Sentence-BERT (SBERT) represent a major practical advance over using plain BERT for semantic search?
options: SBERT invented the Transformer architecture from scratch

SBERT fine-tunes with a siamese structure so each sentence can be embedded independently once in advance, reducing comparison from a full model forward pass per pair to a cheap precomputed vector comparison
SBERT eliminates the need for tokenization entirely
SBERT only works on single words, not full sentences
explanation: Plain BERT requires feeding two sentences together for a similarity score, which is infeasible at scale (a million forward passes to compare one query against a million documents); SBERT's siamese fine-tuning makes precomputed, independent sentence embeddings possible, reducing search to cheap vector comparison.

promptText: In a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline, why is a cross-encoder used only to rerank a small shortlist rather than to search the entire corpus directly?
options: Cross-encoders cannot process more than one document at a time under any circumstances

A cross-encoder requires both texts as joint input for a full forward pass, so its output cannot be precomputed per document ahead of time -- scoring a whole corpus would need one forward pass per document at query time, which doesn't scale
Cross-encoders are less accurate than bi-encoders, so they should only be used as a backup
Cross-encoders can only be run on CPU, making them too slow for any use case
explanation: A cross-encoder's accuracy comes precisely from letting query and document attend to each other jointly, but that also means it cannot be precomputed independently like a bi-encoder; running it over millions of documents at query time is computationally infeasible, so it's reserved for reranking a small post-retrieval shortlist.

promptText: What practical capability does a Matryoshka-trained embedding model provide that a normally-trained embedding model does not?
options: It can process multiple languages simultaneously in a single forward pass

It organizes information hierarchically so a truncated prefix of the vector (e.g., the first 128 of 768 dimensions) remains a coherent, usable embedding, enabling a speed/quality dial without re-running the model
It automatically detects and removes near-duplicate documents from a corpus
It eliminates the need for a vector database entirely
explanation: Matryoshka training applies the contrastive loss at multiple truncation lengths during training, front-loading important information into earlier dimensions, so slicing off trailing dimensions afterward still yields a meaningful (if lower-quality) embedding -- unlike naive truncation of a normally-trained model, which behaves like randomly deleting information.

promptText: Why would a production search system combine dense (embedding) retrieval with sparse (keyword/BM25) retrieval rather than using embeddings alone?
options: Sparse retrieval is always faster and more accurate than dense retrieval in every case

Dense and sparse retrieval fail in complementary ways: embeddings excel at semantic/topical matching but are weak on exact matches (SKUs, error codes, rare proper nouns), while keyword search is the reverse
Combining both methods is required by most vector database vendors' licensing terms
Dense retrieval cannot be used for text at all, only for images
explanation: Embeddings smooth over exact strings and can miss precise identifiers or acronyms, while keyword search is blind to synonyms and paraphrase; hybrid search merges and re-ranks results from both, consistently outperforming either alone on realistic query mixes.

promptText: A team wants to switch their production RAG system to a new, cheaper embedding provider. Why is this fundamentally different from a typical library version bump or config change?
options: It requires re-embedding the entire existing corpus with the new model and validating retrieval quality on a labeled evaluation set before cutover, because embedding spaces from different models are geometrically unrelated and not interchangeable
It is actually identical to a config change since all embedding APIs return vectors in the same shared coordinate space
It only requires updating the API key; the vector database automatically converts vectors between models
It requires no validation because embedding model quality differences are always negligible in practice
explanation: Because embedding spaces are model-specific, old vectors cannot be mixed with new ones -- the migration requires a full corpus re-embed into a parallel index, empirical quality validation against a labeled evaluation set, and a staged cutover, functionally equivalent to a data migration rather than a drop-in swap.

promptText: Why does the rescoring pattern (search with quantized vectors first, then re-rank the shortlist with full-precision vectors) outperform choosing a single precision level for the whole pipeline?
options: Quantization actually improves accuracy uniformly across all comparisons, so rescoring is unnecessary but harmless

It captures most of quantization's cost savings across the bulk of the corpus (which never touches full precision) while avoiding its quality downside where it matters most -- the final ranking decision among close candidates, computed with full-precision data
Full-precision vectors are always faster to search than quantized vectors, so rescoring simply reverses a mistake made earlier
Rescoring eliminates the need for an approximate nearest-neighbor index entirely
explanation: Quantization loss disproportionately harms fine-grained distinctions between candidates that were already close in full precision; a cheap quantized first pass reliably discards the clearly-irrelevant bulk of the corpus, while a full-precision second pass over a small shortlist preserves accurate final ordering -- capturing savings without an all-or-nothing precision trade-off.

promptText: Search relevance visibly degraded shortly after an embedding model upgrade shipped. What is the correct diagnostic order to isolate the root cause?
options: Immediately roll back and assume the new model is permanently worse, without further investigation

First confirm the timeline correlation and rule out unrelated concurrent changes; then check whether the index is a clean full re-embed or a silent mix of old/new-model vectors; then compare the new model against a domain evaluation set; then check for pipeline mismatches like a changed task-prefix or pooling strategy
Immediately increase the embedding dimensionality, since higher dimensionality always fixes relevance regressions
Assume it must be a vector database outage, since embedding models cannot cause search quality regressions
explanation: The investigation should isolate whether the cause is a data problem (mixed/incomplete index -- the most common real-world cause), a model problem (the new model genuinely underperforms on this domain), or an integration problem (pipeline not updated for the new model's requirements), because the fix and urgency differ completely between the three.
